title: Sound Insulation: Key Concepts and Technologies
central_proposition: This chapter comprehensively reviews the critical and evolving field of sound insulation, detailing materials, strategies, experimental methods, and future directions to address noise pollution's impact on public health.

concept_definitions.name: Acoustic materials
concept_definitions.definition: Engineered to mitigate noise by managing sound waves through direction, manipulation, and containment.

concept_definitions.name: Absorber (Sound Absorbing)
concept_definitions.definition: Materials specially designed to reduce noise by absorbing sound waves and converting them into heat, lowering sound levels.

concept_definitions.name: Insulator/Barrier (Sound Blocking or Reflecting)
concept_definitions.definition: Materials designed to control noise in an adjacent medium by obstructing sound waves, optimized to reflect a substantial amount of sound, internally dissipate more sound energy, and transmit the least amount of sound.

concept_definitions.name: Noise Reduction (NR)
concept_definitions.definition: A fundamental metric quantifying a material's ability to decrease sound levels, measuring the difference in sound pressure levels (SPLs) before and after sound interaction.

concept_definitions.name: Insertion Loss (IL)
concept_definitions.definition: A critical performance metric highlighting a material's role in specific acoustic environments, defined as the difference in SPL at a particular point, measured with and without the presence of the acoustic material.

concept_definitions.name: Sound Transmission Loss (STL)
concept_definitions.definition: A comprehensive and crucial metric evaluating acoustic materials, denoting the difference between incident and transmitted sound intensity levels when sound waves encounter a material.

concept_definitions.name: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC)
concept_definitions.definition: A pivotal metric for evaluating acoustic properties, quantifying the ratio of incident sound energy a material absorbs instead of reflecting into the environment.

concept_definitions.name: Sound Transmission Class (STC)
concept_definitions.definition: An essential integer rating for gaging the effectiveness of soundproofing materials in building construction, evaluating a material's ability to reduce sound transmission.

concept_definitions.name: Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC)
concept_definitions.definition: A critical metric quantifying a material's average sound absorption capacity across relevant frequencies, providing a quick and approximate assessment of sound-absorbing effectiveness.

concept_definitions.name: Stiffness Region
concept_definitions.definition: The initial part of the STL curve where a material's sound-blocking ability is influenced by its rigidity, effectively blocking low-frequency sounds.

concept_definitions.name: Resonance Region
concept_definitions.definition: A region in the STL curve marked by variable STL values with pronounced peaks and troughs, corresponding to frequencies where the material's natural vibrations align with sound waves.

concept_definitions.name: Mass Law Region
concept_definitions.definition: A region in the STL curve where heavier barriers are more effective at blocking sound, with STL increasing steadily at higher frequencies.

concept_definitions.name: Coincidence Region
concept_definitions.definition: A region in the STL curve where a noticeable dip occurs at a frequency where the sound wave's wavelength is the same size as the flexural wavelength in the barrier, causing increased sound penetration.

concept_definitions.name: Flanking paths
concept_definitions.definition: Indirect routes for sound transmissions, such as through ceilings, floors, and adjoining walls, allowing sound to bypass a soundproof material.

concept_definitions.name: Metamaterials
concept_definitions.definition: Materials known for their extraordinary ability to manipulate sound wave propagation, sparking interest in acoustic engineering due to their unparalleled STL capabilities.

concept_definitions.name: Perforated Panels
concept_definitions.definition: Panels with holes designed to reduce noise by influencing sound wave behavior, particularly effective for sound absorption and transmission loss.

concept_definitions.name: Polymer Composites
concept_definitions.definition: Materials formed by combining polymers with other substances to enhance acoustic properties, with STL influenced by physical composition and structure.

concept_definitions.name: Recycled or Waste-Derived Materials
concept_definitions.definition: Materials repurposed from waste streams for sound insulation applications, offering sustainable solutions.

argument_structure: The paper systematically reviews the problem of noise pollution, introduces noise control strategies, categorizes acoustic materials, details performance metrics, explains the typical Sound Transmission Loss (STL) curve and its influencing factors, outlines experimental methods and prediction models, presents commercially available and advanced materials, and concludes with practical applications and future directions.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic is that material properties (mass, stiffness, damping, porosity, structure) interact with sound waves (reflection, absorption, transmission) to mitigate noise. This is achieved through physical mechanisms such as converting sound energy to heat, impeding wave propagation, dissipating vibrational energy, manipulating resonance, and engineering structures to control wave behavior, all governed by principles like the mass law and wave-flexural wavelength coincidence.

findings.antecedent: Noise pollution (chronic exposure)
findings.consequent: Detrimental health effects (hearing loss, stress, cardiovascular diseases, cognitive impairment)
findings.mechanism: Chronic noise acts as a stressor, leading to physiological and psychological strain, disrupting cognitive processes and sleep.
findings.source: Abstract, Introduction
findings.quote: highlights the prevalence of noise pollution in urban environments and its diverse detrimental health effects, such as hearing loss, stress, cardiovascular diseases, and cognitive impairment.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Goines and Hagler 2007, Han et al. 2015, Swinburn et al. 2015, WHO and ITU 2019, Smith 1989, Munjal 2013

findings.antecedent: Effective sound insulation materials
findings.mechanism: By blocking or absorbing sound transmission, these materials reduce unwanted noise, creating quieter environments conducive to rest, focus, and personal space.
findings.source: Practical Applications of Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Sound insulation materials are crucial in building construction to reduce noise transmission through walls, floors, and ceilings. This is particularly important in multi-unit residential buildings, hotels, schools, hospitals, and office buildings, where noise reduction contributes significantly to comfort and privacy.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ko et al. 2007, Wester et al. 2009, Maldovan 2013, Zhou et al. 2014, Sung and Kim 2017, Fei et al. 2018, Gulia and Gupta 2018, Haliq et al. 2019, Deuszkiewicz 2021, Sunali et al. 2022, 2024, Ghassabi and Talebitooti 2023, Kinetics noise control 2024

findings.antecedent: Low-demand acoustic environments (e.g., quiet spaces created by sound insulation)
findings.mechanism: Reduced noise levels lower cognitive load and directed attention demands, allowing the Default Mode Network (DMN) to engage in mind-wandering and restorative processes.
findings.source: Practical Applications of Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: In environments like libraries, hospitals, and schools, where quietness is essential, sound insulation materials help create a conducive atmosphere for study, rest, or recuperation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Implicitly supported by ART, though not directly cited in this paper for this specific link.

findings.antecedent: Sustainable and green sound insulation practices (recycled materials, energy-efficient designs, environmentally friendly manufacturing)
findings.mechanism: Utilizing recycled materials, optimizing energy use in design, and employing eco-friendly manufacturing processes directly reduce resource consumption and waste.
findings.source: Sustainable and Green Sound Insulation
findings.quote: Key considerations encompass using recycled materials, adopting energy-efficient designs, and implementing environmentally friendly manufacturing processes, all aimed at minimizing the ecological footprint of sound insulation solutions.

findings.antecedent: Sound-acoustic urban planning, zoning regulations, and architectural innovations
findings.consequent: Noise pollution (mitigated), Quality of life in cities (enhanced)
findings.mechanism: Strategic design and regulation at the urban scale can reduce noise exposure for residents, leading to improved well-being and environmental satisfaction.
findings.source: Evolving Urban Landscapes
findings.quote: The focus is on understanding how urban planning, zoning regulations, and architectural innovations can mitigate noise and enhance the overall quality of life in cities.

findings.antecedent: Evolving noise regulations and standards (local, national, international)
findings.consequent: Design and implementation of sound insulation systems
findings.mechanism: Changes in legal and industry requirements drive innovation and adoption of new materials and methods to meet compliance.
findings.source: Regulatory Changes and Standards
findings.quote: Scientific insights will be crucial in assessing how evolving standards may shape the design and implementation of sound insulation systems in the future.

findings.antecedent: Interdisciplinary collaborations (architecture, engineering, psychology, healthcare)
findings.mechanism: Combining expertise from diverse fields allows for a holistic understanding of noise problems and the development of more comprehensive and effective interventions.
findings.source: Interdisciplinary Collaborations
findings.quote: Exploring the potential of interdisciplinary collaborations, encompassing fields such as architecture, engineering, psychology, and healthcare, in great detail is essential.

findings.antecedent: Absorber materials (porous or fibrous structure)
findings.consequent: Sound energy absorption, low sound reflection and transmission
findings.mechanism: The porous or fibrous structure facilitates the trapping and dissipating of sound waves by converting sound energy into heat.
findings.source: Categories of Acoustic Materials
findings.quote: Typically, these materials possess a porous or fibrous structure that facilitates the trapping and dissipating of sound waves.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ackermann et al. 1988; Kim et al. 2015

findings.antecedent: Insulator/Barrier materials (dense and solid properties)
findings.consequent: Sound reflection, internal sound energy dissipation, minimal sound transmission
findings.mechanism: Their solidity and density are crucial for reflecting and dissipating sound, making them suitable for applications requiring significant noise reduction.
findings.source: Categories of Acoustic Materials
findings.quote: Physically, these materials are dense and solid, typically made from heavy, non-porous substances like mass-loaded vinyl or dense foam. Their solidity and density are crucial for their effectiveness in reflecting and dissipating sound.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wang et al. 2011; Xu et al. 2017

findings.antecedent: Edge-constrained stiff barriers
findings.consequent: Low-frequency sound blocking, higher STL at lower frequencies
findings.mechanism: Rigidity of the material influences its ability to block long-wavelength, low-frequency sounds.
findings.source: Stiffness Region
findings.quote: Edge-constrained stiff barriers effectively block low-frequency sounds with long wavelengths, leading to a higher STL at lower frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Material or structure's natural vibrations align with sound waves (in resonance region)
findings.mechanism: Alignment of natural vibrations with sound waves causes the material to resonate, potentially amplifying sound transmission.
findings.source: Resonance Region
findings.quote: These variations correspond to the frequencies at which the material or structure's natural vibrations align with the sound waves, potentially enhancing sound transmission.

findings.antecedent: Damping (in resonance region)
findings.mechanism: Damping dissipates vibrational energy, smoothing the STL curve and making sound reduction more effective.
findings.source: Resonance Region
findings.quote: This emphasizes the importance of damping in reducing STL fluctuations and improving sound insulation.

findings.antecedent: Mass per unit area of barrier (m) and frequency (f)
findings.mechanism: Heavier barriers are more effective at blocking sound, a property that becomes increasingly pronounced at higher frequencies, as described by the mass law (TLmass = 20 log10(f) + 20 log10(m) – 47.4).
findings.source: Mass Law Region
findings.quote: The underlying principle in the mass law region is that heavier barriers are more effective at blocking sound, a property that becomes increasingly pronounced at higher frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Sound wave's wavelength equals flexural wavelength in barrier (at critical/coincident frequency)
findings.mechanism: This alignment causes the barrier's vibration to resonate with the flexural wave, significantly lowering its sound-blocking capability.
findings.source: Coincidence Region
findings.quote: In the coincidence region, a noticeable dip in the STL curve occurs at a frequency where the sound wave's wavelength is the same size as the flexural wavelength in the barrier, causing increased sound penetration.

findings.antecedent: Density and mass of materials
findings.mechanism: According to the 'mass law' principle, increasing the mass of a barrier increases its ability to block sound.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Heavier and denser materials generally have higher STL. This is attributed to the “mass law" principle, which states that increasing the mass of a barrier increases its ability to block sound.

findings.antecedent: Thickness of a material (with specified density)
findings.mechanism: Thicker barriers can vibrate less easily and, therefore, transmit less sound, especially for lower frequencies.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: The thickness of a material having a specified density is directly proportional to its STL, especially for lower frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Stiffer materials
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) in the coincidence region
findings.mechanism: Stiffer materials can transmit sound more efficiently in the coincidence region, leading to lower STL.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Stiffer materials can transmit sound more efficiently in the coincidence region, leading to lower STL.

findings.antecedent: Internal damping (e.g., rubber, foam, fiberglass)
findings.consequent: Sound energy conversion to heat, sound transmission
findings.mechanism: Materials with higher internal damping can convert more sound energy into heat, thus reducing sound transmission.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Materials with higher internal damping can convert more sound energy into heat, thus reducing sound transmission.

findings.antecedent: Material's resonant frequency
findings.mechanism: Every material has a resonant frequency at which it vibrates most efficiently, amplifying sound and reducing its STL.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Every material has a resonant frequency at which it vibrates most efficiently. The material can amplify sound at this frequency, reducing its STL.

findings.antecedent: Environmental factors (temperature and humidity)
findings.consequent: Physical properties of materials, Sound Transmission Loss (STL)
findings.mechanism: These factors can change the physical properties of materials, affecting their STL, e.g., higher humidity can affect sound propagation by changing sound speed.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: These environmental factors can change the physical properties of materials, affecting their STL.

findings.antecedent: Frequency of sound
findings.mechanism: Materials exhibit varying STL characteristics across different frequencies, being more effective at blocking high-frequency sounds but less effective at low frequencies, or vice versa.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Materials exhibit varying STL characteristics across different frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Improper installation (gaps, holes, poor seals)
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) of a barrier
findings.mechanism: How a material is installed can significantly impact its sound transmission properties; improper installation can significantly undermine the STL of a barrier.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: How a material is installed can significantly impact its sound transmission properties. Improper installation, characterized by gaps, holes, or poor seals, can significantly undermine the STL of a barrier.

findings.antecedent: Composite materials (e.g., layers of different materials)
findings.mechanism: Each layer can be engineered to target specific frequencies or sound types for enhanced sound insulation.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Using composite materials (e.g., layers of different materials) can enhance STL, as each layer can be engineered to target specific frequencies or sound types for enhanced sound insulation.

findings.antecedent: Sound bypassing through 'Flanking paths'
findings.consequent: Effectiveness of a material in blocking sound
findings.mechanism: Sound can bypass a soundproof material through indirect routes for sound transmissions, reducing its effectiveness.
findings.source: Factors Affecting the Sound Transmission Loss of Materials
findings.quote: Sound can bypass a soundproof material through “Flanking paths,” which refers to indirect routes for sound transmissions, such as through ceilings, floors, and adjoining walls.

findings.antecedent: Metamaterial-based thin plates with subwavelength resonator arrays
findings.mechanism: These engineered structures exhibit higher STL than conventional bare plates, particularly for low-frequency sound insulation.
findings.source: Metamaterials
findings.quote: Metamaterial-based thin plates equipped with subwavelength resonator arrays exhibit higher STL than conventional bare plates, showcasing their effectiveness in low-frequency sound insulation.

findings.antecedent: Damping within metamaterials
findings.consequent: Vibroacoustic attenuation performance, Sound Transmission Loss (STL)
findings.mechanism: Damping plays a critical role in dissipating vibrational energy, impacting the overall vibroacoustic attenuation and STL of metamaterials.
findings.source: Metamaterials
findings.quote: The critical role of damping within metamaterials for vibroacoustic attenuation performance, particularly the impact of damping in resonators and host structures on STL, is highlighted.

findings.antecedent: Lightweight multilayer honeycomb membrane-type acoustic metamaterials
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) while maintaining low weight
findings.mechanism: These materials defy the traditional mass law by achieving exceptional STL through their engineered structure, despite being lightweight.
findings.source: Metamaterials
findings.quote: Lightweight multilayer honeycomb membrane-type acoustic metamaterials (Fig. 5a) defy the traditional mass law to achieve exceptional STL while maintaining a low weight.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic metamaterials incorporating piezoelectric patches
findings.mechanism: Piezoelectric patches provide dual functionality, allowing the material to both attenuate sound and convert mechanical vibrations into electrical energy.
findings.source: Metamaterials
findings.quote: Acoustic metamaterials incorporating piezoelectric patches offer dual functionality in sound insulation and energy harvesting, achieving over 20 dB STL and a maximum energy conversion efficiency of up to 15.3%.

findings.antecedent: Helmholtz cavity-based acoustic metamaterials
findings.consequent: Sound insulation performance (particularly for low-frequency noise)
findings.mechanism: The specific design of Helmholtz cavities enables exceptional sound insulation, especially in isolating low-frequency noise.
findings.source: Metamaterials
findings.quote: Helmholtz cavity-based acoustic metamaterials demonstrate exceptional sound insulation performance, particularly in isolating low-frequency noise.

findings.antecedent: Metamaterial barriers based on cellular structures
findings.consequent: High Sound Transmission Loss (STL) in the low-frequency range
findings.mechanism: Cellular structures provide high STL without the need for excessive mass, particularly effective at low frequencies.
findings.source: Metamaterials
findings.quote: Metamaterial barriers based on cellular structures (Fig. 5b) provide high STL in the low-frequency range without the addition of excessive mass.

findings.antecedent: Perforation diameter (of perforated-natural fiber sandwich panels)
findings.mechanism: The size of perforations significantly impacts how sound waves interact with the panel, affecting its STL.
findings.source: Perforated Panels
findings.quote: The STL of perforated-natural fiber sandwich panels is notably influenced by perforation diameter.

findings.antecedent: Small perforations in corrugated sandwich panels
findings.consequent: Low-frequency sound absorption and transmission loss
findings.mechanism: Small perforations modify the acoustic impedance and create resonant effects that improve sound absorption and transmission loss at low frequencies.
findings.source: Perforated Panels
findings.quote: Small perforations in corrugated sandwich panels significantly enhance low-frequency sound absorption and transmission loss.

findings.antecedent: Panel's perforation rate and elastic properties (of underwater flexible micro-perforated panels)
findings.mechanism: These properties dictate how the panel vibrates and interacts with sound waves, thereby affecting its sound insulation capabilities.
findings.source: Perforated Panels
findings.quote: Underwater flexible micro-perforated panels (Fig. 7) show that the panel's perforation rate and elastic properties significantly influence STL.

findings.antecedent: Micro-perforated panels coupled with honeycomb panels (considering air cavities)
findings.mechanism: The combination of micro-perforated panels, honeycomb structures, and air cavities creates a system that effectively attenuates sound at mid-frequencies through resonance and impedance mismatch.
findings.source: Perforated Panels
findings.quote: Micro-perforated panels coupled with honeycomb panels consider air cavities for offshore plants, showing a significant increase in STL at mid-frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Increased glass bead volume fraction and sound frequency (in inorganic particulate-filled polymer composites)
findings.mechanism: Higher volume fraction and frequency enhance the material's ability to block sound transmission.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: STL increases with the glass bead volume fraction and sound frequency.

findings.antecedent: Increased size of glass beads (in inorganic particulate-filled polymer composites, constant volume fraction)
findings.mechanism: Larger bead sizes, for a constant volume, may reduce the composite's effectiveness in blocking sound.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: However, it decreases when the size of the glass beads is increased, given a constant volume fraction.

findings.antecedent: Addition of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) into Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) composites
findings.mechanism: CNTs increase the stiffness of the composite, which contributes to enhanced STL.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: The addition of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) into Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) composites has been shown to significantly enhance STL, a benefit attributed to the increased stiffness provided by the CNT additives.

findings.antecedent: Particle type and composite structure (in polymer/inorganic particle composites)
findings.mechanism: The specific type of particles and how they are structured within the polymer matrix critically influence the composite's acoustic properties.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Further investigations into polymer/inorganic particle composites, such as PP/nano-CaCO3, ABS/CaCO3, and PVC/hollow glass bead (HGB), have confirmed the significant role of particle type and composite structure on STL.

findings.antecedent: Adding CNTs and foaming to wood fiber-low-density polyethylene (LDPE) composites
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) at medium and higher frequencies
findings.mechanism: CNTs and foaming modify the material's structure and mechanical properties, enhancing its ability to block sound, particularly at higher frequencies.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Moreover, adding CNTs and foaming to wood fiber-low-density polyethylene (LDPE) composites has improved STL, especially at medium and higher frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Hybrid composites (flax fabric + polypropylene + carbon fibers)
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) per areal density
findings.mechanism: The hybrid structure provides superior acoustic performance compared to traditional materials like aluminum, with further improvements upon hybridization.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Hybrid composites, particularly those reinforced with flax fabric and polypropyl-ene (PP) hybridized with carbon fibers (Fig. 8), have demonstrated STL per areal density significantly higher than traditional materials like aluminum, with further improvements upon hybridization.

findings.antecedent: Optimizing carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites
findings.consequent: Transmission loss levels comparable to traditional metal materials (especially at lower frequencies)
findings.mechanism: Careful design of CFRP composites allows them to match or exceed the acoustic performance of metals, particularly for low-frequency sound insulation.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Optimizing carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites can achieve transmission loss levels comparable to traditional metal materials, especially at lower frequencies.

findings.antecedent: PP/clay/CNT nanocomposites
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) at both high and low frequencies
findings.mechanism: The synergistic effects of clay and CNTs within the polypropylene matrix enhance the material's ability to block sound across a broad frequency range.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Synergistic effects on STL have been observed in PP/clay/CNT nanocomposites, with the STL for these composites significantly outperforming pure PP at both high and low frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Composite rubber reinforced with hollow glass microspheres (HGM)
findings.consequent: Noise reduction capabilities and sound insulation performance
findings.mechanism: The incorporation of HGM provides optimal weighted STL, leading to promising noise reduction and excellent sound insulation.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Research on composite rubber reinforced with hollow glass microspheres (HGM) indicates promising noise reduction capa-bilities and excellent sound insulation performance, with optimal weighted STL achieving significant levels under various thickness constraints.

findings.antecedent: Polymer nanocomposites with nano-clay particles and nanofibers in polyurethane foam
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) and absorption coefficient
findings.mechanism: The inclusion of nano-clay particles and nanofibers enhances the material's ability to both block and absorb sound energy.
findings.source: Polymer Composites
findings.quote: Furthermore, enhancing polymer nanocomposites with nano-clay particles and nanofibers in polyurethane foam can increase STL and the absorption coefficient.

findings.antecedent: Increased rubber crumb content and PMDI adhesive (in wood-waste tire rubber composite panels)
findings.mechanism: The composition of the panels, particularly the amount of rubber crumb and adhesive, directly influences their soundproofing capabilities.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Key findings include the observation that increasing the rubber crumb content and the level of PMDI adhesive in the WRCP enhances its sound insulation properties.

findings.antecedent: Optimal densities (in inorganic polymeric foams from metakaolin and blast furnace slag)
findings.mechanism: Achieving optimal density in these foams enhances their structural properties to effectively block sound transmission.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: They observed significant STL improvements in IPFs with optimal densities, demonstrating their potential as sound-insulating mate-rials in construction and building applications.

findings.antecedent: Natural and hard-processed woods
findings.consequent: Sound absorption (poor), Sound barriers (effective), Transmission loss (up to 70 dB)
findings.mechanism: The inherent properties of these woods make them less effective at absorbing sound but good at blocking it due to their density and structure.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: It found that natural and hard-processed woods were generally poor sound absorbers but effective sound barriers, with maximum transmission loss up to approximately 70 dB.

findings.antecedent: Adding coconut fiber filter mats (to hard-processed wood)
findings.mechanism: The fibrous structure of coconut fiber mats enhances the sound-absorbing properties of the composite material.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Adding materials like coconut fiber filter mats significantly improved sound absorption in hard-processed wood.

findings.antecedent: Cork (soft processed wood)
findings.consequent: Sound absorption (mid-frequency ranges), Transmission loss (up to 40 dB)
findings.mechanism: Cork's inherent properties allow for good sound absorption at mid-frequencies and acceptable sound blocking.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Cork, classified as a soft processed wood, showed better sound absorption at mid-frequency ranges (500 Hz to 2000 Hz) and had acceptable transmission loss of up to 40 dB.

findings.antecedent: Waste rubber geopolymer concrete (WRGC)
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) and sound absorption properties
findings.mechanism: The novel composition of WRGC, incorporating waste rubber, enhances its acoustic performance compared to conventional concrete.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: The study reveals that waste rubber geopolymer concrete (WRGC) exhibits superior STL and better sound absorption properties than conventional concrete.

findings.antecedent: Increased NRCs (in waste rubber geopolymer concrete)
findings.consequent: Effectiveness as a sound barrier material
findings.mechanism: Higher Noise Reduction Coefficients directly indicate improved sound absorption and barrier capabilities.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: It demonstrates increased NRCs, indicating its effectiveness as a sound barrier material.

findings.antecedent: Olive stone-filled PP, gypsum boards, and wood fiber-reinforced PP
findings.mechanism: The incorporation of olive stone flour into these composites influences their acoustic performance.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Naghmouchi et al. (2016) focused on the soundproofing characteristics of olive stone-filled PP, gypsum boards and wood fiber-reinforced PP.

findings.antecedent: Smaller WPCB particle sizes and higher WPCB mass ratios (in WPCB-UP composites)
findings.consequent: Surface density and stiffness, sound insulation
findings.mechanism: These material properties contribute to the composite's ability to block sound transmission.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: They found that smaller WPCB particle sizes and higher WPCB mass ratios in the composite enhance surface density and stiffness, contributing to better sound insu-lation.

findings.antecedent: Recycled ABS reinforced with short cotton fiber waste
findings.mechanism: The composite exhibits high STL due to the combined acoustic properties of recycled ABS and cotton fibers.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: The research reveals that these composites exhibit substantial STL, with the highest mean value reaching around 70 dB.

findings.antecedent: Increasing micronized rubber powder (MRP) content (in pine particleboard)
findings.mechanism: MRP alters the mechanical properties of the particleboard, making it less rigid but more pliable.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: The study found that increasing MRP content decreased the strength and increased the flexibility of the particleboards.

findings.antecedent: MRP addition (to pine particleboard)
findings.mechanism: MRP provides minor acoustic benefits, primarily in sound blocking rather than absorption.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Acoustically, MRP addition slightly improved STL but did not significantly enhance sound absorption compared to the control sample.

findings.antecedent: LCW-based panels (from recycled leather cutting waste)
findings.consequent: Sound absorption capabilities (0.2 to 0.7 in mid-frequency range), Sound Transmission Loss (STL) (up to 30 dB)
findings.mechanism: The material properties of recycled leather cutting waste allow for effective sound absorption and blocking.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: The results indicate that the LCW-based panels exhibit significant sound absorption capabilities, with absorption coefficients ranging from 0.2 to 0.7 in the mid-frequency range. The STL values are up to 30 dB, demonstrating their effec-tiveness in sound insulation.

findings.antecedent: Composite insulation panels (from recycled cotton fibers and polyethylene/PP packaging wastes)
findings.consequent: Sound Transmission Loss (STL) (8 dB), Thermal resistance (0.11 m²°C/W)
findings.mechanism: The combination of recycled cotton fibers and plastic wastes creates a material with effective acoustic and thermal insulation properties.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: The panels demonstrated notable STL, reaching 8 dB, and improved thermal resistance, with a value of up to 0.11 m²°C/W.

findings.antecedent: Composite materials (expanded perlite, natural polymers, and rapeseed waste)
findings.consequent: Sound absorption coefficients at various frequencies
findings.mechanism: The unique combination of these waste-derived materials enhances their ability to absorb sound energy across different frequencies.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: The study showcases significant improvements in sound absorption coefficients at various frequencies, highlighting the composites' potential for noise reduction.

findings.antecedent: Adding HEP waste (to fired clay bricks), orientation and proportion of waste
findings.mechanism: The inclusion and arrangement of high-energy propellant waste within bricks modify their acoustic properties, influencing STL.
findings.source: Recycled or Waste-Derived Sound Insulation Materials
findings.quote: Specifically, bricks with HEP waste exhibited changes in STL, with directional orientation during baking influencing acoustic performance.

methodological_critiques: Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC) may not accurately represent a material's performance at very low or very high frequencies.
The mass law model's effectiveness significantly diminishes above a material's 'critical frequency'.

Empirical models' reliability and precision are contingent upon the quality and pertinence of the underlying data, limiting their accuracy to conditions and materials analogous to those represented in the dataset.
Machine learning models' prediction quality is highly dependent on the quality and quantity of the training data.
model_structure: The paper reviews existing models for predicting Sound Transmission Loss (STL), including the Mass Law model, Spring-Mass model, Finite Element Analysis (FEA), Statistical Energy Analysis (SEA), Empirical models, Machine Learning models, Wave-based models, and Transfer Matrix Method (TMM). It also presents the Source-Path-Receiver model as a general framework for noise control strategies.
limitations: NRC may not accurately represent a material's performance at very low or very high frequencies.
The mass law model's effectiveness significantly diminishes above the material's 'critical frequency'.
Empirical models' reliability and precision are contingent upon the quality and pertinence of the underlying data, circumscribing accuracy to analogous conditions/materials.
Machine learning models' prediction quality is highly dependent on the quality and quantity of training data.

paper_metadata.title: A Developmental Framework for Embodiment Research: The Next Step Toward Integrating Concepts and Methods
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A Developmental Framework for Embodiment Research: The Next Step Toward Integrating Concepts and Methods
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Embodiment research is at a turning point. There is an increasing amount of data and studies investigating embodiment phenomena and their role in mental processing and functions from across a wide range of disciplines and theoretical schools within the life sciences. However, the integration of behavioral data with data from different biological levels is challenging for the involved research fields such as movement psychology, social and developmental neuroscience, computational psychosomatics, social and behavioral epigenetics, human-centered robotics, and many more. This highlights the need for an interdisciplinary framework of embodiment research. In addition, there is a growing need for a cross-disciplinary consensus on level-specific criteria of embodiment. We propose that a developmental perspective on embodiment is able to provide a framework for overcoming such pressing issues, providing analytical tools to link timescales and levels of embodiment specific to the function under study, uncovering the underlying developmental processes, clarifying level-specific embodiment criteria, and providing a matrix and platform to bridge disciplinary boundaries among the involved research fields.
